name: stress
prose: Static test helper taking a fixture cfix and a worker function. When FEATURE_THREADS is defined it runs ptu_test(ptunit_thrd_create, &cfix->thrd, worker, cfix) in a loop num_threads times, so every thread handle is stored through the same &cfix->thrd (the fixture keeps a handle; what happens to earlier handles is not checked here) and the return values of the spawned workers are not examined here. Then, in all builds, it calls worker(cfix) in the calling thread and checks ptu_int_eq(errcode, 0). It ends with return ptu_passed(). The ptu_test and ptu_int_eq macros are defined in ptunit headers that are not in this source tree; they are the places where a thread-creation failure or a nonzero worker result is reported, and, as is usual for such macros, a failed assertion is expected to return a failed result from stress instead of reaching the final return, but I could not read their definition to confirm that.

Reviewer round1 (worker return values in spawned threads not checked, handles kept in cfix->thrd) right; round15 (claim of always returning ptu_passed is wrong because ptu_* assertions can fail) right in substance: prose no longer says "always"; macro behaviour unverified (ptunit.h not in tree).

name: main
prose: Program entry of editmap (a sendmail map editor); the slice cut the head, K&R definition at editmap.c:74. It zeroes the SMDB params (cache size 1 MB), derives progname, sets RunAsUid/RealUid and gid from getuid/getgid, fills RealUserName from getpwuid (or "Unknown UID n"), and parses options "C:fquxN" (-C config file, -f no case folding, -q query, -u update, -x remove, -N include the terminating NUL in key and value, anything else calls usage). It adds SFF_* flags depending on the DontBlameSendmail bits, then requires exactly one of -q/-u/-x and the matching operand count (query and remove need exactly 3 operands after the options, update needs more than 3) or calls usage. It takes type, map name and key (and value for update), lower-cases the key unless -f. With HASFCHOWN it opens the sendmail.cf file (exit EX_NOINPUT if it cannot be opened) and scans for an O TrustedUser line to set TrustedUid. It opens the map with smdb_open_database (read-only for query; read/write and create otherwise); on failure it prints a message (with a recompile hint for an unsupported type) and exits EX_CANTCREAT. It syncs the database, and if geteuid() == 0 and TrustedUid != 0 it tries to change the owner (failure only prints a warning). Query: smdb_get; any error (not only not-found) prints a message and sets exit status EX_UNAVAILABLE, otherwise it prints the value. Update: smdb_put; failure prints a message and sets EX_IOERR. Remove: smdb_del; SMDBE_NOT_FOUND prints a message but leaves the status EX_OK, SMDBE_OK is silent, any other error prints a message and sets EX_IOERR. It then closes the database (close failure prints a message and sets EX_IOERR), frees it and calls exit(exitstat). It does not return normally.

name: mi_milteropen
prose: K&R function mi_milteropen(conn, backlog, rmsocket, name) that creates, binds and listens on the milter socket described by conn ("protocol:filename" or "protocol:port@host" or a bare address); slice cut the head, function starts at listener.c:122. It returns the listening socket or INVALID_SOCKET. It returns INVALID_SOCKET if conn is NULL or empty; if the protocol part is unknown or no default protocol is available; for AF_UNIX if the path is too long or safefile reports it as unsafe; for inet/inet6 if the port is neither numeric nor a known service name or the host cannot be parsed or resolved; if socket() fails; if setting close-on-exec or SO_REUSEADDR fails (the socket is closed); if rmsocket is set and the path exists but stat fails with an error other than ENOENT, is not a socket, or cannot be unlinked (socket closed); if bind or listen fails (socket closed); and if malloc of the global sockpath for the UNIX path fails (socket closed). On success for a UNIX socket it stores a copy of the path in the global sockpath. The function modifies the caller's conn string in place by temporarily writing NUL at the ':' and at the '@'. The ':' is restored only on the success path of the protocol parse, so returning for an unknown protocol leaves a NUL there; the '@' is restored only after the port has been parsed, so returning for an invalid port or unknown service name leaves a NUL there. Sets the global L_socksize and may set other listener globals.

name: mi_listener
prose: K&R function mi_listener(conn, dbg, smfi, timeout, backlog): the milter accept loop. It calls mi_opensocket and, when _FFR_WORKERS_POOL is compiled in, mi_pool_controller_init; either failure returns MI_FAILURE immediately (these early returns do not reach the smutex_destroy of L_Mutex at the end). Then, while mi_stop() returns MILTER_CONT, it locks L_Mutex and selects on listenfd with a MI_CHK_TIME timeout: an invalid listenfd, a select exception on the socket, MAX_FAILS_S select failures (EINTR just retries) , MAX_FAILS_A accept failures, MAX_FAILS_M malloc failures or MAX_FAILS_T thread-creation failures set ret to MI_FAILURE and leave the loop; a timeout loops again. After accept it closes and rejects the connection if the client address looks incomplete or the descriptor is not usable with select, and for transient accept errors (EINTR, EAGAIN, ECONNABORTED, EMFILE, ENFILE, ENOBUFS, ENOMEM, ENOSR, EWOULDBLOCK) it just continues without counting. Accepted connections get close-on-exec and SO_KEEPALIVE (failures only logged) and a freshly malloced context (if malloc fails the socket is closed), whose callback mask is filled from smfi, and it starts a session (mi_start_session or thread_create; a failure closes the socket and frees ctx). After the loop, if ret is not MI_SUCCESS it calls mi_stop_milters(MILTER_ABRT), otherwise it logs a stop/abort message if mi_stop was not MILTER_CONT and calls mi_closener. It then destroys L_Mutex and returns ret. I did not read mi_opensocket, mi_stop or the session-start helpers.

Reviewer original (omits MI_FAILURE on corrupted listenfd and select exception) right; round15 (early returns do not destroy L_Mutex) right.

name: smfi_setreply
prose: K&R function smfi_setreply(ctx, rcode, xcode, message) that stores a custom SMTP reply in ctx->ctx_reply. It returns MI_FAILURE, leaving ctx->ctx_reply unchanged, if rcode or ctx is NULL; if rcode is not exactly 3 characters long; if rcode does not start with '4' or '5' followed by two ASCII digits; if xcode is non-NULL but myisenhsc(xcode, NUL) rejects it (it must start with 2, 4 or 5, a dot, 1 to 3 digits, a dot, 1 to 3 digits and then the end of the string, so its length is between 5 and 9 characters); if message is non-NULL and contains CR or LF or is longer than MAXREPLYLEN; or if malloc fails. Otherwise it builds the string "rcode ", then xcode if given, then (a space only when xcode was given, then) message if given, frees any previous ctx->ctx_reply, stores the new buffer there and returns MI_SUCCESS. The caller keeps ownership of the argument strings; ctx owns the new buffer.

name: smfi_setmlreply
prose: smfi_setmlreply(ctx, rcode, xcode, ...) stores a multi-line SMTP reply in ctx->ctx_reply from a NULL-terminated list of text arguments. It returns MI_FAILURE, leaving ctx->ctx_reply unchanged, if rcode or ctx is NULL; if rcode is not exactly 3 characters or does not start with '4' or '5' followed by two digits; if xcode is non-NULL and myisenhsc(xcode, NUL) rejects it (otherwise "4.0.0" or "5.0.0" is used depending on the first digit of rcode); if any text argument is longer than MAXREPLYLEN or contains CR or LF, or if more than MAXREPLIES text arguments are given (the scan stops at the first such argument and the call fails); or if malloc fails. Otherwise it allocates a buffer sized for the code, xcode and each line, writes "rcode-xcode" or "rcode xcode" (the separator is a space only when exactly one text argument was counted, otherwise a hyphen), then " first text" and for each further text argument CRLF, the code and separator (space for the last line) and the text, frees any previous ctx->ctx_reply, stores the buffer there and returns MI_SUCCESS. With zero text arguments the stored string is rcode, a hyphen and xcode with no text.

name: sm_heap_report
prose: Writes a report of the heap-checking tables to a stream; slice cut the head and the definition is at heap.c:758. It is compiled only in the branch of the #if at line 114 that applies when SM_HEAP_CHECK is nonzero (the #else at line 212 up to the #endif at 837, whose comment says !SM_HEAP_CHECK for the enclosing test), and at run time it returns immediately without writing anything if HEAP_CHECK (sm_debug_active(&SmHeapCheck, 1)) is false or verbosity <= 0. Otherwise it walks every entry of SmHeapTable: with verbosity > 2 it prints one line per entry (group, pointer, size, optional tag and number), with verbosity exactly 2 only entries whose group is not 0, and with verbosity 1 none; it totals sizes by group 0, group 1 and other groups. It then reads the current time, formats it into a static buffer with localtime (the result of localtime is not checked for NULL), prints a summary line with pid, time, SmHeapMaxTotal, the grand total and group totals, and prints a "BUG" line if the grand total differs from SmHeapTotal. Returns nothing and does not change the heap tables; it does change the function-static time string.

Reviewer round15 (code under !SM_HEAP_CHECK writes summary but annotation says nothing written) wrong: the function is in the #else branch of #if !SM_HEAP_CHECK, so it is compiled only when SM_HEAP_CHECK is on; the nothing-written case is the runtime HEAP_CHECK/verbosity test.

name: sm_io_setvbuf
prose: sm_io_setvbuf(fp, timeout, buf, mode, size) sets the buffering of an SM_FILE_T. It first requires fp to have SmFileMagic (SM_REQUIRE_ISA). If mode is not SM_IO_NBF, a mode other than SM_IO_FBF, SM_IO_LBF or SM_IO_NOW, or size > INT_MAX, returns SM_IO_EOF with fp not yet touched. Otherwise it converts the timeout, flushes the old buffer with sm_flush (result ignored), frees any unread-pushback buffer, clears f_r and f_lbfsize, frees the old buffer only if it was malloced (flag SMMBF; a buffer supplied by an earlier caller is not freed), and clears the buffering and EOF flags. With SM_IO_NBF it switches to unbuffered mode (one-byte f_nbuf buffer) and returns 0. Otherwise it asks sm_whatbuf for the optimal size; size 0 means use that size with a library-allocated buffer; if buf is NULL it sm_mallocs size bytes: if that fails it remembers SM_IO_EOF as the result and, if size differs from the optimal size, retries with the optimal size; if still no buffer it switches to unbuffered mode and returns SM_IO_EOF; if the retry succeeds the stream is left buffered with the optimal size and the function returns SM_IO_EOF. A buffer it allocated is marked SMMBF. It then sets SMNPT if the size differs from the optimal size, sets the line/now/full flag for mode, installs the buffer, sets f_w or f_lbfsize for write streams (f_w = 0 for read streams), registers sm_cleanup with atexit and returns 0 (or SM_IO_EOF after a successful retry).

Reviewer original (a successful allocation retry still returns SM_IO_EOF and leaves a buffered stream, not an unbuffered one) right; round15 (old buffer freed only if malloced) right: previous prose said it was always freed.

name: sm_io_fopen
prose: sm_io_fopen(pathname, flags, ...) opens a file with open(2) and wraps it in an SM_FILE_T of type SmFtStdio. Slice cut the head; the packet name sm_sysfopen does not exist in libsm, the code shown is the tail of sm_io_fopen (head at stdio.c:470). If flags contains O_CREAT it reads the mode argument with va_arg, else mode is 0. It maps the access mode in flags (O_RDONLY, O_WRONLY, O_RDWR) to SMRD, SMWR or SMRW; any other value calls sm_abort. It obtains a stream with sm_fp(SmFtStdio, ioflags, NULL) (its result is used without a NULL check) and sets fp->f_file to open(pathname, flags, mode). If open returns -1 it clears the stream flags and magic so the slot is unused and returns NULL; otherwise it returns the new stream. It does not itself set f_cookie or do any buffering setup beyond what sm_fp does.

name: sm_strseek
prose: sm_strseek(fp, offset, whence) repositions a string-backed stream. It computes a target ret from whence: SM_IO_SEEK_SET gives offset, SM_IO_SEEK_CUR gives the current strio_offset plus offset, SM_IO_SEEK_END gives strio_size (the offset argument is not added in the code). Any other whence sets errno to EINVAL and returns -1. If ret is negative or exceeds (size_t)-1 it returns -1 without setting errno. If ret is greater than the current strio_size it calls sm_strgrow(s, ret): on success it recomputes (goto reseek) with the same arguments, on failure it returns -1 (errno set by sm_strgrow). Otherwise it stores ret in strio_offset and returns it.

name: notify_rd
prose: Test receiver for the sm_notify mechanism, notify_rd(nproc, nmsgs). It calls sm_notify_start(true, 0); if that is negative it prints a perror message and returns -1. Then it loops nmsgs * nproc times; in each iteration it calls sm_notify_rcv with a 5 second timeout, recording SM_TEST(r >= 0) each time, and repeats while the result is 0; if the result is negative it prints a diagnostic and returns that negative value at once. A received message is NUL-terminated at buf[r] when r < sizeof(buf) and at the last byte of buf, then checked with SM_TEST for: prefix "qf0001", length greater than the prefix, a decimal pid after the prefix that validpid() maps to an index below nproc, a '_' followed by a message number n with 0 <= n < nmsgs, and msgs[pidx][n] being NUL before it is set to 'f'. The SM_TEST checks only record failures; they do not change the return value. After the loop it returns 0. Global state used or changed: the msgs table, Verbose, stderr output, and whatever sm_notify_start sets up.
note: t-notify.c:98-162 (start failure 107-112, receive loop 114-126, checks 135-158, return 161). Reviewer original (prose omits sm_notify_start failure and says it returns 0 despite SM_TEST failures) right; round2/round15 (formal contract too weak) right: contract removed because the function uses globals and I/O.

name: sm_vfscanf
prose: sm_vfscanf(fp, timeout, fmt0, ap) is the scanf-style scanner on an SM_FILE_T; slice cut the head, the function starts at vfscanf.c:109. A timeout of SM_TIME_DEFAULT becomes fp->f_timeout; if the timeout is SM_TIME_IMMEDIATE it sets errno to EAGAIN and returns SM_IO_EOF without reading. For other finite timeouts it arms an alarm event via sm_seteventm and a setjmp(ScanTimeOut): if the alarm fires it sets errno to EAGAIN and returns SM_IO_EOF (this path does not clear the event itself). It then walks the format: when the format string ends it clears the event and returns nassigned (which can be 0). Whitespace in the format skips input whitespace; literal characters must match the next input character or the scan stops with match failure; a '%' followed by NUL clears the event and returns SM_IO_EOF; conversions that need input first try to refill the buffer and go to input failure at end of input. Conversions store through pointers taken from ap and each stored one increments nassigned (%n stores the count of characters read and does not count). A match failure (for example no digits for a number, an empty %[ set, or a literal mismatch) clears the event and returns nassigned. Input failure (end of file or error before a conversion could start) clears the event and returns nassigned if it is non-zero, otherwise -1. I read the control flow and returns, not every conversion body in the 600-odd lines.
note: vfscanf.c:109-758 (timeout 136-158, format end return nassigned at 167-171, '%' then NUL return SM_IO_EOF at 318-321, input_failure 750-753 returns nassigned ? nassigned : -1, match_failure 754-757 returns nassigned). Reviewer round15/round17 (normal end of format with zero assignments returns -1) wrong: the format-end return at 171 gives nassigned (0 if nothing assigned); -1 comes only from input failure with nothing assigned. Name in the packet was a placeholder; the function is sm_vfscanf.

name: smdb_cdb_open
prose: smdb_cdb_open(database, db_name, mode, mode_mask, sff, type, user_info, db_params) opens a cdb map (only compiled with CDB defined); slice shows only the tail of the function at smcdb.c:428-566. It sets *database to NULL, then builds the file name with the extension (error returned), calls smdb_setup_file (error returned) and smdb_lock_file (error returned); if the file did not exist and O_CREAT is in mode it will truncate instead of create (mode |= O_TRUNC, clears O_CREAT and O_EXCL). It allocates the SMDB_DATABASE and cdb map objects; if either allocation fails it unlocks the lock file, frees what was allocated and returns SMDBE_MALLOC. It opens the file with open(file name, mode, DBMMODE): failure gives SMDBE_BAD_OPEN via the error exit. It sets cdbmap_create for a non-read-only mode and calls cdb_init (O_RDONLY) or cdb_make_start (other modes); a nonzero result gives SMDBE_BAD_OPEN via the error exit; otherwise result is set to SMDBE_OK (the else branch at 521-527 can never run because result is 0 there) and smdb_filechanged is called. If that returns SMDBE_OK it installs the smcdb_* method pointers in the database object, stores sm_cdbmap in smdb_impl, sets *database and returns SMDBE_OK. Any other result falls to the error exit, which unlocks the lock file through sm_cdbmap->smcdb_lock_fd, frees sm_cdbmap, frees the database object with smdb_free_database and returns the result; the opened db_fd is not closed there (the close is only a comment).

name: smdb_lockfile
prose: smdb_lockfile(fd, type) tries to lock a file descriptor and returns a bool. On systems without flock (!HASFLOCK) it builds an fcntl lock request from type (LOCK_UN gives F_UNLCK, LOCK_EX gives F_WRLCK, otherwise F_RDLCK) and uses F_SETLK for LOCK_NB, F_SETLKW otherwise; with flock it calls flock(fd, type). Either way it retries while the call fails with EINTR. It returns true if the call succeeds (this includes a successful LOCK_UN unlock, so true does not necessarily mean a lock was acquired); in the fcntl variant it also returns true when the call fails with EINVAL. Otherwise it returns false with errno set to the saved error: in the fcntl variant any failure other than EINVAL, and in the flock variant any failure, ends at a return false (the explicit conditions about LOCK_NB with EACCES/EAGAIN or EWOULDBLOCK only decide whether the unused debug code path is taken; both paths set errno = save_errno and return false). EINTR is not returned as the final error. It opens, closes and allocates nothing.
note: smdb.c:80-157 (fcntl variant 86-133, flock variant 134-153, final return false 155-156). Reviewer round15 (returns true for a successful LOCK_UN unlock too) right; earlier mechanical contract complaints moot (contract not given).

name: smdb_ndbm_open
prose: smdb_ndbm_open(database, db_name, mode, mode_mask, sff, type, user_info, db_params) opens an ndbm map; the packet name smndbm_open does not exist, the function is at smndbm.c:488-630. It sets *database to NULL and returns SMDBE_UNKNOWN_DB_TYPE if type is NULL; calls smdb_setup_file for the .dir and then the .pag extension (an error is returned); remembers lockcreated if either file does not exist and O_CREAT is in mode; locks the .dir file with smdb_lock_file (error returned). If the files are being created it also locks and closes the .pag file with O_EXCL semantics (on failure it closes the .dir lock descriptor and returns the error) and changes mode to O_TRUNC without O_CREAT/O_EXCL. It allocates the database and dbm wrapper objects (an allocation failure only sets result to SMDBE_MALLOC; it does not return at once). If result is still SMDBE_OK it stores the lock descriptor and calls dbm_open(db_name, mode, DBMMODE): failure gives the errno value or SMDBE_BAD_OPEN. It then fails with SMDBE_GDBM_IS_BAD if the dir and pag descriptors are the same, and runs smdb_filechanged on both files. If everything succeeded it fills in the smdbm_* method table, stores the wrapper in smdb_impl, sets *database and returns SMDBE_OK. Otherwise it closes dbm if opened, unlocks via db->smndbm_lock_fd, frees db and the database object and returns result; this error path dereferences db without a NULL check, so it is a NULL dereference if smdbm_malloc_database failed.

name: rebuildaliases
prose: rebuildaliases(map) rebuilds the alias database for map and returns true only if the rebuild ran. It returns false at once if the map class is not MCF_REBUILDABLE. It adds safe-file flags from the DontBlameSendmail settings and opens the alias file with safefopen for read/write; if that fails and errno is EACCES or EROFS it tries a read-only open (and, in that case, will skip locking); if both opens fail, or the first fails with another errno, it logs (message unless the map is optional) and returns false. Unless locking is skipped it takes an exclusive non-blocking lock on the file; if that fails it prints a message, waits for the other rebuild by locking with LOCK_EX unless OpMode is MD_INITALIAS, closes the file and returns false. It then calls the class map_open with O_RDWR: if it succeeds it logs (when LogLevel > 7), marks the map MF_OPEN|MF_WRITABLE, records map_pid, calls readaliases (which returns nothing, so no result is checked) and sets success to true; if it fails it prints a diagnostic and success stays false. It closes the alias file, and if the map is flagged MF_OPEN it calls map_close and clears MF_OPEN|MF_WRITABLE|MF_CLOSING. It returns success. The early return false paths (not rebuildable, open failure) happen before the file is opened or the map is touched; the lock-failure path closes the file but does not change the map flags. The success can therefore be true even when the file was opened read-only without a lock.

Reviewer original (can return true without locking via read-only fallback) right; round15 (early returns do not close file or clear flags, contradicting every path) right: the earlier prose's every-path claim removed.

name: load_if_names
prose: Void, takes no arguments; the packet name was a placeholder and the function is load_if_names at conf.c:4832 (slice 4893-5147 is only its middle). It enumerates the machine's network interfaces and adds their IP addresses to class $=w and calls add_hostnames for each usable one. In the IPv6/SIOCGLIFCONF build (4834-5077) it creates a datagram socket (returns silently if that fails), obtains the interface count (SIOCGLIFNUM/SIOCGIFNUM where compiled; if the count is not positive it closes the socket and returns), reads the SIOCGLIFCONF list (failure: close and return), and for each entry it closes and recreates the socket for the address family (returns if that fails), skips entries whose family is not AF_INET or AF_INET6, and, only where SIOCGLIFFLAGS is compiled, skips entries when the flags ioctl fails or IFF_UP is not set. For an IPv6 address it prints a warning and skips the interface if the address is unspecified; for an IPv4 address it warns and skips if it is INADDR_ANY or INADDR_NONE; otherwise the text form "[addr]" is built, and if it is not yet in class w it is added with setclass. Then, only where SIOCGLIFFLAGS is compiled, if DontProbeInterfaces is DPI_SKIPLOOPBACK and IFF_LOOPBACK is set it skips the interface before add_hostnames (the loopback address text has already been added to class w by then); otherwise add_hostnames(sa) is called. At the end it frees the buffer and closes the socket. In the non-IPv6 SIOCGIFCONF build (5078-5300) the structure is the same with SIOCGIFFLAGS/IFF_UP and IFF_LOOPBACK checks; I read that half only by its returns and conditions.
note: conf.c:4832-5300 (IPv6 variant 4834-5077: socket 4863-4865, count 4893-4896, conf 4905-4912, per-entry flags 4981-5001, AF_INET6 5008-5040, AF_INET 5042-5055, class w 5061-5066, loopback skip 5068-5073, add_hostnames 5074). Partly read: the non-IPv6 half (5078-5300) and the ifdef-selected buffer setup were skimmed. Reviewer round17 (UP and loopback filtering only under SIOCGLIFFLAGS/SIOCGIFFLAGS) right.

name: hostnamebyanyaddr
prose: hostnamebyanyaddr(sap) returns a printable host name for a socket address, a pointer that the caller must not free as if it were its own allocation (it can point to static storage or, see below, to whatever denlstring returned). The packet name hostnamebyaddr does not exist; the function is at daemon.c:4651-4751. With NAMED_BIND it temporarily shortens the resolver retry count so retry*retrans does not exceed 20 (at least 1) and restores it after the lookup. It calls sm_gethostbyaddr according to sa_family (AF_INET, AF_INET6, AF_ISO where compiled, AF_UNIX gives no host entry, other families use sa_data). If a host entry was found, its name does not start with '[' and it is not a literal IPv6 address (inet_pton) and not a literal IPv4 address (inet_addr), the name is passed through denlstring(name, true, true) and returned; in IPv6 builds, if denlstring returned the same pointer as h_name the name is first copied into a function-static MAXNAME buffer and the host entry is freed, so the returned name is that static buffer or whatever denlstring returned otherwise. In builds without NETINET6 the entry is not freed there and the returned pointer is the denlstring result (possibly pointing into the resolver's own storage). Otherwise it frees the host entry (FREEHOSTENT), returns "localhost" for an AF_UNIX address whose path starts with NUL, and else formats "[address]" with anynet_ntoa into a function-static 203-byte buffer and returns it. I did not read denlstring.

name: starttls
prose: starttls(m, mci, e, implicit, [DANE args]) performs the client side of STARTTLS and returns an exit status; the packet name starttlsclt does not exist, the function is at deliver.c:7481-7742. It returns EX_TEMPFAIL if the client TLS context is NULL and initclttls(true) fails, if TLS_set_engine fails, or if SSL_new fails. It then calls get_tls_se_features: a non-EX_OK result is the return value after the fail label frees the SSL object. Unless implicit it sends STARTTLS and reads the reply: a 4xy reply gives EX_TEMPFAIL, a reply of -1 gives -1, a 5xy reply gives EX_UNAVAILABLE, any other reply that is not 220 gives EX_PROTOCOL (all via the fail label). It stores the TLS info with SSL_set_ex_data (failure is a fail exit) and, with DANE compiled in, may enable DANE and set the SNI host name (failures there are logged or only affect the DANE flags, not the result), sets SNI for STS if configured, sets the read and write descriptors (failure is a fail exit), and runs SSL_connect, retrying through tls_retry while that says to retry; if the connect finally fails it logs and takes the fail exit. After a successful connect it stores the SSL object in mci->mci_ssl, calls tls_get_info (its result is not examined) and sfdctls to switch the streams to TLS; if sfdctls returns 0 it returns EX_OK. At the fail label it frees clt_ssl with SM_SSL_FREE and returns EX_SOFTWARE if the status variable is still EX_OK, else that status; because mci->mci_ssl was assigned before sfdctls, a sfdctls failure leaves mci->mci_ssl pointing at the freed SSL object.

name: sendenvelope
prose: sendenvelope(e, mode) (void) delivers or verifies the recipients of an envelope. It returns without doing anything else except setting EF_CLRQUEUE when e has EF_FATALERRS and OpMode is MD_SMTP or MD_DAEMON. It returns silently, with no other change, if the envelope is not EF_RESPONSE and the return-to-sender timeout for its class is NOW, or a deliver-by return time has already passed. Otherwise it zeroes e_nsent, sets EF_GLOBALERRS, defines the {envid} and {bodytype} macros and, if e is not already split (EF_SPLIT), saves e_sibling, clears it, calls split_by_recipient(e) (if that returns false and EF_FATALERRS is set it sets EF_CLRQUEUE in SMTP and daemon modes and returns, leaving e_sibling as split_by_recipient left it), queues up each new sibling, then closes the transcript, unlocks the queue and drops the data file of each sibling and restores e_sibling to the saved list (this restore is skipped on the early return). It then loops over e->e_sendqueue: in SM_VERIFY mode it only sets e_to and prints a "deliverable" message for addresses for which QS_IS_SENDABLE holds (not for every address); otherwise, for addresses with QS_IS_OK state, it checkpoints the queue every CheckpointInterval sent addresses (queueup, resetting e_nsent) and calls deliver(e, q) (result ignored). If any address was delivered it sets e_dtime to now and increments e_ntries.

name: main
prose: main(argc, argv, envp) is sendmail's entry point (main.c:163-3024, about 2900 lines). Partly read: I read the part shown in the slice and the main control skeleton to the end (queue-run branch, daemon startup, getrequests and the final send loop) by control flow only; the option parsing, configuration reading and initialisation in the first ~2100 lines were not read. From the part read: in the one-shot queue-run case the process labels itself "Queue control", resets SIGCHLD to the default, and while CurChildren > 0 it waits with sm_wait (stopping early if wait fails with ECHILD, ignoring stopped children, otherwise calling proc_list_drop) and then calls finis(true, true, ExitStat), which does not return. If OpMode is MD_DAEMON or QueueIntvl > 0 it forks into the background unless run_in_foreground or the debug flag 99.100 is set (a fork failure is a syserr; the parent of a successful fork calls finis(false, true, EX_OK)), records daemon information, and if QueueIntvl > 0 starts the queue runner (runqueue, or run_work_group for a specific queue group); in non-daemon mode with persistent queue runners it then monitors the runner children itself and finally calls finis(true, true, ExitStat). Otherwise, for MD_SMTP or MD_DAEMON it goes on to serve requests through getrequests (which returns in a child process unless the 93.100 debug flag is set). Later parts include a verify-mode branch, calls to finis(true, true, EX_USAGE) on collection errors, a send loop calling sendall, a final adjustment of ExitStat to EX_USAGE if Errors > 0 and ExitStat is EX_OK, and the final finis(true, true, ExitStat) with a return of ExitStat that is only reached if finis returns. Most paths therefore end in finis rather than returning.

Reviewer round15 (daemon parent fork path ends via finis(false,true,EX_OK)) right; round17 (tTd(99,100) fork exception, and runqueue only if QueueIntvl > 0) right (2389, 2461). Earlier prose (specific early-return exit codes for -bS, frozen config and -L) was not checked by me and is dropped.

name: milter_data
prose: milter_data(e, state) runs the end-of-message phase of every input milter and returns the reply text (or NULL) while storing the final disposition in *state. It first sets *state to SMFIR_CONTINUE itself, so no caller precondition on *state is needed. For each filter in InputFilters it stops the loop if *state is already something other than continue or accept; resets *state to continue; skips a filter whose connection is closed or not in the open/in-message state (a filter in error state is handled through MILTER_CHECK_ERROR or ends the loop); sets mf_state to SMFS_INMSG; sends headers (unless SMFIP_NOHDRS), the end-of-headers command (unless SMFIP_NOEOH), and the body (unless SMFIP_NOBODY or there is no data file), checking the results after each (MILTER_CHECK_RESULTS, which I did not read); sends the end-of-body command and reads replies until *state leaves continue, a read error occurs, or the EOM timeout expires (then milter_error and the loop ends). Replies handled: replycode, reject, discard and tempfail set *state and mark the filter done; continue and accept set *state to accept (or tempfail if a body replacement failed) and mark it done; progress does nothing; quarantine stores the reply text (an empty string if none) in e->e_quarmsg and the {quarantine} macro; add/insert/change header, change sender, add recipient (with or without parameters) and delete recipient are applied even if the filter did not declare the capability (only logged); replace body is rejected and marked as a failed replacement if the filter lacks the capability, otherwise the data file is reopened on first use and replaced chunk by chunk; any other reply is logged and milter_error is called. After each reply that is not a replycode the response buffer is freed and set to NULL, so the quarantine empty string does not survive as the return value. After the loop, if a replacement failed, *state becomes tempfail when it was continue or accept, and the reopened data file is closed and EF_HAS_DF cleared. Then it resets or rewinds the data file as needed; if that fails it sets ExitStat to EX_IOERR, forces tempfail when the state was continue or accept, and calls syserr. It finishes with MILTER_CHECK_DONE_MSG and returns response, which, from the reply loop, is non-NULL only when the last processed reply was a replycode (response values set by the MILTER_CHECK_RESULTS macros before the loop were not examined).
note: milter.c:4344-4754 (*state set 4363, loop 4372-4705, reply switch 4496-4682, response freed 4683-4687, finishup 4707-4748, return 4753). Reviewer original (omits caller guarantee *state == SMFIR_CONTINUE) wrong: the function sets it at 4363; round15 (quarantine with no reply leaves an empty response so the return may be non-NULL) wrong: lines 4683-4687 free and NULL the response after any non-replycode reply.

name: mime7to8
prose: mime7to8(mci, header, e) rewrites a 7-bit encoded text/plain body (base64 or quoted-printable) as 8-bit while writing it to the mailer connection; the function starts at mime.c:1033 (slice cut the head). It looks up the Content-Transfer-Encoding header value and parses it with prescan. If the header is missing or cannot be parsed it calls syserr, sets EF_DONT_MIME, writes the header "Content-Transfer-Encoding: value" only when a value exists (so a missing header produces no CTE line), writes an empty line to end the headers, clears MCIF_INHEADER, copies the whole data file with putxline using PXLF_MAPFROM, and returns true (false if any write fails). Otherwise it copies the encoding name, sets MCIF_INHEADER, writes "Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit" and an "X-MIME-Autoconverted: from <cte> to 8bit by <host> id <id>" header and the blank line, clears MCIF_INHEADER, then decodes the body from e->e_dfp: base64 (read four characters at a time, skipping whitespace, handling '=' padding) or, for any other encoding, quoted-printable (soft line breaks and =XX escapes), writing each decoded line with putxline. It finishes with an extra empty line (the decoded text may lack a final newline) and returns true; a write failure at any putline or putxline goes to the writeerr label and returns false. I read the control flow and returns, not each decoding step.

name: invalidaddr
prose: invalidaddr(addr, delimptr, isrcpt) checks the address string for bad characters and for excessive length and returns true if it is invalid, false otherwise; the function starts at parseaddr.c:277 (slice cut the head). If delimptr is non-NULL it saves *delimptr and, if that is not NUL, writes NUL there so the scan ends at delimptr; the saved character is written back at the end (including after the too-long exit) when delimptr is non-NULL and the saved character was not NUL. It scans addr in place. In builds without USE_EAI, when EightBitAddrOK is false each byte in the 0x80-0x9f range calls setstat(EX_USAGE), sets the result to true and permanently overwrites that byte with BAD_CHAR_REPLACEMENT in the caller's string; this happens before the length test for the same byte. It counts length with XLEN and as soon as the count exceeds MAXNAME - 1 it temporarily NULs the current byte, prints "553 5.1.0 Address ... too long" with usrerr, restores the byte, sets the result to true and jumps to the exit (skipping the 501 message). If the scan finished and the result is true it prints one 501 error naming the address, code 5.1.3 when isrcpt is set and 5.1.7 otherwise. In USE_EAI builds there is no 8-bit replacement in the loop. It returns the result.

name: occ_close
prose: occ_close(e, mci, host, addr) decrements the open-connection count for a connection that was counted. It returns false at once if the global occ is NULL or e is NULL, or if mci is NULL, is in MCIS_CLOSED state, is flagged MCIF_CACHED, or does not have MCIF_OCC_INCR set. Otherwise it clears MCIF_OCC_INCR in mci_flags, takes the current time, runs conn_limits(e, now, addr, SM_CLFL_EXC, occ, -1, -1) between SEM_LOCK and SEM_UNLOCK (the result of conn_limits is ignored; the semaphore macros are compiled in only with _FFR_USE_SEM_LOCKING and SM_CONF_SEM, and I did not read whether they skip locking when no semaphore is available) and returns true. The host argument is not used.

name: split_by_recipient
prose: split_by_recipient(e) splits an envelope into siblings by queue group and by recipient count. It returns true immediately if OpMode == SM_VERIFY (as written in the code), the envelope's queue group is not valid, or EF_SPLIT is already set. Otherwise it calls split_across_queue_groups(e): SM_SPLIT_FAIL returns false. It remembers firstsibling = e->e_sibling, optionally allocates a log buffer for the new envelope ids (only if n > 1 and LogLevel is high), and for each of the n - 1 siblings calls split_within_queue(ee): on SM_SPLIT_FAIL it sets e->e_sibling back to firstsibling, frees the log buffer and returns false (changes made by earlier splits, including split_across_queue_groups and previously split siblings, are not undone); otherwise it sets EF_SPLIT on that sibling and appends its id to the log text. It then logs the split (if enabled), calls split_within_queue(e) for the envelope itself, sets EF_SPLIT on e if that did not fail, and returns whether it did not fail. When it returns false in the last step e_sibling is not restored.

name: dsntoexitstat
prose: dsntoexitstat(dsncode) maps the leading part of an enhanced status code string to an exit status; it reads the string beyond its first character, so it needs a NUL-terminated string. If the first character is '2' it returns EX_OK, if '4' EX_TEMPFAIL, and if it is not '5' EX_CONFIG. For '5' it skips an optional '.', reads the next number code2, skips to the next '.', reads code3, and switches on code2: 0 gives EX_UNAVAILABLE; 1 (address) gives by code3 0 EX_DATAERR, 1 or 6 EX_NOUSER, 2 or 8 EX_NOHOST, 3 or 7 EX_USAGE, 4 EX_UNAVAILABLE, 5 EX_CONFIG; 2 (mailbox) gives 0, 1, 2, 4 EX_UNAVAILABLE and 3 EX_DATAERR; 3 gives EX_OSERR; 4 (network/routing) gives 0 and 2 EX_IOERR, 1, 3, 5 EX_TEMPFAIL, 4 EX_PROTOCOL, 6 EX_CONFIG, 7 EX_UNAVAILABLE; 5 gives EX_PROTOCOL; 6 gives EX_UNAVAILABLE; 7 gives EX_DATAERR. A first character of '5' with any code2 or code3 not listed for it falls to the final return EX_UNAVAILABLE.

name: udbexpand
prose: udbexpand(a, sendq, aliaslevel, e) tries to expand address a through the user database. Partly read: the control flow and returns were read, but the UDB_DBFETCH, UDB_HESIOD and UDB_FORWARD bodies only partly in detail (the DB version ifdefs were skimmed). It returns EX_OK without changes if a is not QS_IS_SENDABLE, if UdbSpec is empty, if the user name starts with a backslash or a colon, or if the key would not fit in the key buffer; it sets e->e_to to the address text when sendable. It returns EX_TEMPFAIL if the one-time _udbx_init(e) returns EX_TEMPFAIL, or a database or Hesiod lookup fails with a temporary error. It then loops over the UdbEnts. For a UDB_DBFETCH entry it looks up the key "user:maildrop"; if found it clears QSELFREF, and if EF_VRFYONLY is set it sets q_state QS_VERIFIED and returns EX_OK, otherwise it expands the stored value with sendtolist, logs, and sets q_state QS_EXPANDED when addresses were produced and the address is not marked as a self reference; it also looks up "user:mailname" to set q_owner and marks the address QDELIVERED|QEXPANDED when it finds one. When the lookup finds nothing (UDB_DBFETCH), it breaks out of that entry at once, before the QSELFREF clear and without changing q_state, and the loop moves to the next entry. The UDB_HESIOD case does the same through Hesiod; UDB_FORWARD handles forward entries and can set QS_VERIFIED (returning EX_OK in verify-only mode) or QS_EXPANDED; UDB_REMOTE does nothing here. After the loop it returns EX_OK, so a no-match, remote or self-reference outcome returns EX_OK without setting QS_VERIFIED or QS_EXPANDED.

Reviewer original (returns EX_OK on no-match, remote or selfref without setting QS_VERIFIED or QS_EXPANDED) right; round15 (NEWDB no-match still clears QSELFREF so the address is not unchanged) wrong for the UDB_DBFETCH no-match path: it breaks at line 253 before the clear at line 260.

name: smtpinit
prose: smtpinit(m, mci, e, onlyhelo) (void) starts an SMTP/LMTP session on an open connection. It sets SmtpNeedIntro, clears e_rcode/e_renhsc/e_text and resets map-changed flags, then switches on mci->mci_state: MAIL, RCPT or DATA first call smtprset and fall through to OPEN; OPEN returns at once if onlyhelo is false (no greeting or HELO is exchanged), and continues if onlyhelo is true; ERROR, QUITING and SSD call smtpquit and fall through; CLOSED calls syserr("451 4.4.0 smtpinit: state CLOSED") and returns without calling smtpquit; OPENING continues. With onlyhelo it jumps straight to the HELO/EHLO step; otherwise it sets MCIS_OPENING and reads the greeting: a read failure (r < 0) goes to tempfail1, a 4xy reply to tempfail2 and any non-2xy reply to unavailable. It then sends LHLO, EHLO or HELO according to the mailer and retry rules, and reads the reply: failure goes to tempfail1, a 5xy reply to unavailable (or retries with HELO when falling back), another non-2xy reply to tempfail2. It checks the host name in the greeting and, if the mailer is not exempt and the name equals MyHostName, reports a 553 config loop error, records EX_CONFIG and calls smtpquit. If configured it sends VERB (failure goes to tempfail1). If the state is not CLOSED it sets MCIS_OPEN and returns. tempfail1 and tempfail2 record EX_TEMPFAIL (4.4.2 and 4.5.0) and call smtpquit unless the state is CLOSED; unavailable records EX_UNAVAILABLE (5.5.0) and calls smtpquit. The function returns nothing; results are recorded in mci status. I did not read the HELO name expansion and the extension parsing between 160-250 in detail.
note: usersmtp.c:95-314 (state switch 132-159, greeting 163-182, EHLO/HELO 189-247, loop check 255-268, VERB 277-286, open 288-291, tempfail/unavailable 296-313). Reviewer original (onlyhelo skips greeting; OPEN with !onlyhelo returns without exchange) right; round15 (CLOSED logs 451 but does not call smtpquit) right.

name: attemptauth
prose: attemptauth(m, mci, e, sai) tries one SASL mechanism and returns an exit status; it is compiled only with SASL. It sets (*sai)[SASL_MECH] to NULL at the start (before a mechanism is chosen), disposes of any existing mci_conn, creates a new client connection with sasl_client_new (failure returns EX_TEMPFAIL), sets security properties with SASL_SEC_NOPLAINTEXT and the external SSF/auth id and the IP properties (each sasl_setprop failure returns EX_TEMPFAIL), and calls sasl_client_start against the server's mechanism list; a result other than SASL_OK or SASL_CONTINUE returns EX_TEMPFAIL (logging when no mechanism qualifies). It stores the chosen mechanism in (*sai)[SASL_MECH], sends "AUTH mech" with or without an initial response (a base64 encoding failure returns EX_TEMPFAIL), and then loops: reply 235 records {auth_type} and returns EX_OK; reply -1 returns EX_IOERR; a 5xy reply returns EX_NOPERM; any other reply that is not 3xy returns EX_TEMPFAIL; for a 3xy reply it calls sasl_client_step: if that fails (not OK or CONTINUE) it sends "*" to abort, reads the reply and returns EX_NOPERM (not EX_TEMPFAIL); if base64 encoding of the step output fails it sends "*" and returns EX_TEMPFAIL; otherwise it sends the encoded response and reads the next reply. The loop has no other exit.
note: usersmtp.c:1610-1917 (mech reset 1637, client_new 1651-1661, setprop 1672-1763, client_start 1789-1802, AUTH send 1806-1840, loop 1850-1915: EX_OK 1857, EX_IOERR 1860, EX_NOPERM 1862, EX_TEMPFAIL 1867, step failure EX_NOPERM 1893, encode failure EX_TEMPFAIL 1904). Reviewer original (omits EX_NOPERM/EX_IOERR paths; sets SASL_MECH NULL before selection) right; round15 (client step failure returns EX_TEMPFAIL, not EX_NOPERM) wrong: it returns EX_NOPERM at line 1893 (only the base64 failure returns EX_TEMPFAIL).

name: smtpauth
prose: smtpauth(m, mci, e) runs SMTP AUTH using attemptauth and returns an exit status; compiled only with SASL. It clears mci->mci_sai, calls getauth: EX_TEMPFAIL is returned at once; if getauth returned EX_OK but gave no SASL_AUTHID it returns EX_OK without authenticating and without setting mci_sasl_auth; if getauth did not return EX_OK it returns EX_UNAVAILABLE when SASLInfo is NULL, otherwise it calls readauth and returns its result if that is not EX_OK. It returns EX_UNAVAILABLE if the password is empty, or if both the authid and the user are empty. It fills the callback contexts, sets a default realm and mechanism list, intersects the mechanism list with the server's capabilities, and calls init_sasl_client (failure returns EX_TEMPFAIL if getauth supplied the data, else EX_UNAVAILABLE). Then it loops calling attemptauth: EX_OK sets mci_sasl_auth to true and ends the loop; EX_TEMPFAIL or EX_NOPERM removes the failed mechanism from mci_saslcap and, if none are left, returns that result when getauth supplied the data or EX_UNAVAILABLE otherwise, else tries the next mechanism; any other result is returned at once (without removing a mechanism). It returns the final result, EX_OK on success.
note: usersmtp.c:1945-2039 (getauth 1958-1965, readauth 1966-1977, checks 1980-1987, init 2017-2019, loop 2020-2037). Reviewer original (returns EX_OK without mci_sasl_auth when getauth yields no AUTHID) right; round15 (not every failure removes the mechanism: early getauth/readauth/init and EX_IOERR returns do not) right.

name: smtpmailfrom
prose: smtpmailfrom(m, mci, e) sends MAIL FROM and returns an exit status; the function starts at usersmtp.c:2055 (slice cut the head). If mci_state is MCIS_CLOSED it sets errno from mci_errno and returns EX_TEMPFAIL without recording a status. It returns EX_DATAERR (after usrerrenh and mci_setstat EX_NOTSTICKY) when the message needs SMTPUTF8 and it is disabled or not offered by the server, or when 8-bit data is present and the server does not support 8BITMIME; it builds the option string (SIZE, BODY, DSN, AUTH and others) and the sender address, sets mci_state to MCIS_MAIL, sends MAIL From:<addr> options, and reads the reply: r < 0 records EX_TEMPFAIL (4.4.2) and returns EX_TEMPFAIL; SMTPCLOSING returns EX_TEMPFAIL; a 4xy reply records EX_NOTSTICKY and returns EX_TEMPFAIL; a 2xy reply returns EX_OK; 501 and 553 record EX_NOTSTICKY and return EX_DATAERR; 552 records EX_NOTSTICKY and returns EX_UNAVAILABLE (and may clear the size option flag); any other 5xy reply records EX_NOTSTICKY and returns EX_UNAVAILABLE; any other reply logs, records EX_PROTOCOL (5.5.1), calls smtpquit and returns EX_PROTOCOL. Partly read: the option-string construction in 2085-2290 was not read line by line.

Reviewer round15 (EX_PROTOCOL/smtpquit path and status recording on the closed-connection path not present) mixed: the EX_PROTOCOL plus smtpquit path exists (2362-2365), but the closed-connection path records no status, as the reviewer says.

name: smtprcpt
prose: smtprcpt(to, m, mci, e, ctladdr, xstart) sends RCPT TO for one recipient and returns an exit status; the function starts at usersmtp.c:2384. With PIPELINING it first reads any replies already waiting: while mci_nextaddr is non-NULL and the input is readable it calls smtprcptstat for that address, and on a non-EX_OK result calls markfailure and giveresponse for it, then advances mci_nextaddr (e_to is restored afterward). If mci_state is MCIS_CLOSED it sets errno from mci_errno and returns EX_TEMPFAIL directly, before any smtprcptstat call for this recipient. It builds the NOTIFY/ORCPT option string for DSN-capable servers, sends "RCPT To:<addr>options", sets mci_state to MCIS_RCPT, and, when pipelining is enabled (MCIF_PIPELINED set), returns EX_OK without reading the reply; otherwise it returns smtprcptstat(to, m, mci, e), whose result can be EX_TEMPFAIL (state closed or a 4xy/failed read), EX_OK (2xy), EX_NOUSER, EX_UNAVAILABLE (other 5xy) or EX_PROTOCOL (after recording the protocol error). name: smtpdata
prose: smtpdata(m, mci, e, ctladdr, xstart) sends the DATA command and message body and returns an exit status; the function starts at usersmtp.c:2652. If mci_state is MCIS_CLOSED it returns EX_TEMPFAIL (it does not require the connection to be open). With PIPELINING it first drains the pending RCPT replies, calling smtprcptstat for each, markfailure and giveresponse on failures and setting QS_RETRY on EX_TEMPFAIL ones; if the connection closed meanwhile it returns EX_TEMPFAIL. It sends DATA, sets MCIS_DATA and reads the reply: r < 0 or a 4xy reply returns EX_TEMPFAIL (calling smtpquit in the failed-read case); a 5xy reply returns EX_TEMPFAIL if no recipients were accepted (mci_okrcpts <= 0) and mci_retryrcpt is set, else EX_UNAVAILABLE; any other reply that is not 3xy records EX_PROTOCOL and returns EX_TEMPFAIL under the same no-recipients-and-retryrcpt condition, else EX_PROTOCOL. If mci_okrcpts > 0 it writes the message body with a write timeout; a write failure ends at the writeerr label (errno saved, MCIS_ERROR, EX_TEMPFAIL or EX_NOTSTICKY recorded, data file rewound, syserr 451 message, smtpquit, return EX_TEMPFAIL). A reply arriving before the final dot gives EX_PROTOCOL with MCIS_ERROR and smtpquit, and an error on the final flush gives EX_IOERR with MCIS_ERROR and smtpquit. After the final dot it returns EX_OK without a reply when no recipients were sent; otherwise it reads the final reply: failure gives EX_TEMPFAIL, 4xy EX_TEMPFAIL, 2xy EX_OK, a protocol error EX_PROTOCOL, 5xy EX_UNAVAILABLE and anything else EX_PROTOCOL (the final-dot paths do not apply the retryrcpt rule), recording the mci status and the status message. Partly read: the body-writing section 2767-2850 was only skimmed by its returns.

name: xconnect
prose: xconnect(inchannel) handles sendmail's X-CONNECT (and optionally HAProxy PROXY) preamble and returns an int; the function is at util.c:3042-3257 (packet name xconnect_handler does not exist). It consults the x_connect ruleset with rscap on the peer name and address: EX_UNAVAILABLE or any other non-EX_OK status returns 0 (the latter also logged), and a result starting with CANONNET returns 0. With _FFR_HAPROXY a ruleset result "haproxy1" selects PROXY mode. With _FFR_XCNCT > 1 a ruleset result starting "220" makes it print a 220- greeting line and flush OutChannel. It then reads one line from InChannel with the to_nextcommand timeout. In PROXY mode it returns -1 if the line is NULL or does not start with "PROXY ", returns -2 for "UNKNOWN" (logged and ignored), and accepts "TCP4 " or "TCP6 " (otherwise returns -1); in the normal mode it returns -1 unless the line starts with "X-CONNECT ", then skips spaces. It reads an address token of alphanumerics, '.' and ':', and accepts an IPv4 address (inet_addr) or an IPv6 address (inet_pton, if compiled); any other token returns -1, and on success the address is copied into RealHostAddr. In PROXY mode it skips the destination-address token and takes the port from the next token (the source port) into RealHostAddr, frees RealHostName and returns D_XCNCT. Otherwise, if the address token is not followed by a space it returns D_XCNCT; else it reads a host name token (letters, digits, '.', '-'), returns D_XCNCT if it is empty, replaces RealHostName with a copy of the name, and if no space follows returns D_XCNCT; if the rest of the line starts with 'M' it returns D_XCNCT_M, otherwise D_XCNCT.

name: nbns_rq
prose: nbns_rq(rqp) sends a NetBIOS name service request and parses the reply header; the function is at nbns_rq.c:329-381. It sets rqp->nr_if to the global interface list head and calls nbns_rq_opensocket (an error is returned at once); then it loops with retrycount 3: nbns_rq_send (an error is returned at once), nbns_rq_recv; if recv fails with an error other than ETIMEDOUT or no retries remain, then for a broadcast request (NBNS_NMFLAG_BCAST) with a next interface it closes nr_fd, advances to the next interface and restarts from opening a socket, otherwise returns that error (which can be ETIMEDOUT, an errno, or -1 from select inside recv); on an ETIMEDOUT with retries left it decrements the count and sends again, so there are up to four send/receive attempts per interface. After a received reply it returns NBERROR(NBERR_INVALIDRESPONSE) if the reply is shorter than 12 bytes or its transaction id differs from nr_trnid. It then parses the flags into nr_rpnmflags and nr_rprcode (returning NBERROR(nr_rprcode) if the response code is non-zero), skips the question count and reads the answer, authority and additional counts into nr_rpancount, nr_rpnscount and nr_rparcount, and returns 0. The mb_get_* return values are not checked. nr_fd is not closed on the success or error returns (only before moving to the next interface).

name: smb_open_rcfile
prose: smb_open_rcfile() reads the smb configuration files and returns an errno-style int. It takes $HOME, and if set builds "$HOME/.nsmbrc" in a malloc'ed buffer (malloc result unchecked), calls rc_open on it in read mode into the global smb_rc and frees the buffer; its result is only stored in a local variable and is overwritten. It then calls rc_merge(SMB_CFG_FILE, &smb_rc), again without checking the result, and if smb_rc is still NULL it prints "Warning: no cfg file(s) found." with printf and returns ENOENT; otherwise it returns 0. It never returns the rc_open or rc_merge error codes.

The "never returns" wording is limited to this function's own returns: it only returns ENOENT or 0.

name: ScanOneEntry
prose: Static helper of Jim's scan command: ScanOneEntry(interp, str, pos, str_bytelen, fmtObj, idx, valObjPtr) scans one format entry against str. It first sets *valObjPtr to 0. If the entry has a prefix it matches it against str from pos (whitespace in the prefix skips any whitespace in the input): it returns -1 if the input is used up, and 0 if the prefix did not match completely. Unless the type is 'c', '[' or 'n' it skips whitespace; then for 'n' it stores the current position as an integer object; otherwise if the input is exhausted it returns -1; for 'c' it stores the next UTF-8 character code as an integer object and returns the number of bytes consumed since the entry start. For other types it optionally limits the token to the field width (a temporary string object), and converts: d, o, x, u, i parse an integer (base 10, 8, 16, 10 and auto), e, f, g parse a double; on success the value object is stored and the consumed count includes the characters converted, on failure to convert the result is 0 if there is remaining text and -1 if the token is empty. s and [ use JimScanAString with the entry's character-set argument, set *valObjPtr to the string it returns (an empty string object, not NULL, if no characters match) and add its length. A temporary width-limited object is freed before returning. It returns the number of bytes consumed from anchor (including leading whitespace), 0 for a mismatch, or -1 at end of input.

name: Jim_EvalObj
prose: Jim_EvalObj(interp, scriptObjPtr) evaluates a script object and returns a Jim return code. If the object is a list with no string representation it returns JimEvalObjList(interp, scriptObjPtr) at once (not read here). Otherwise it increments the script object's reference count, gets the parsed script with JimGetScript and, if the parse reports a missing closing delimiter (JimParseCheckMissing returns JIM_ERR), sets the error stack, drops the reference and returns JIM_ERR; so an unparseable script returns JIM_ERR. It then sets an empty interpreter result; with JIM_OPTIMIZATION it returns JIM_OK immediately for an empty script (result stays empty) and has a fast path for a three-token "incr var" script on an unshared integer variable, which increments the variable in place, sets it as the result and returns JIM_OK. Otherwise it marks the script in use, pushes an eval frame, clears errorFlag and evaluates each command line: it builds argv from the line's words (string/escape tokens as they are, variables via Jim_GetVariable, expression sugar and nested [commands] evaluated recursively, dict sugar, interpolated words, and {*} expansion of lists), stops the loop as soon as retcode is not JIM_OK or a word could not be produced (then retcode becomes JIM_ERR if it was OK), and for each complete line calls JimInvokeCommand and then JIM_SIGNAL if Jim_CheckSignal reports a signal. The result code of the last command is propagated, so JIM_RETURN, JIM_BREAK, JIM_CONTINUE, JIM_EXIT, JIM_ERR and JIM_SIGNAL are returned as they occur; the loop ends after the first non-OK code. It releases the argument references and any heap-allocated argv per line, sets the error stack when the code is JIM_ERR, pops the eval frame, converts the object back to a script type holding the parsed script, drops its reference and returns the code.

name: JimCallProcedure
prose: JimCallProcedure(interp, cmd, argc, argv) calls a Tcl-style procedure and returns a Jim return code. It returns JIM_ERR (after JimSetProcWrongArgs sets the error message) if the argument count is below the required arity, or above required plus optional arity when the procedure has no args parameter, before any frame exists; returns JIM_OK at once if the body is empty (no frame created, procLevel not changed); returns JIM_ERR with "Too many nested calls. Infinite recursion?" if the current frame level equals maxCallFrameDepth (again before any frame exists). Otherwise it creates a call frame (argv, argc, argument and body objects, static variables), increments interp->procLevel, increments the references of the argument list and body, makes the new frame current, and binds the parameters in order: an args parameter receives the remaining arguments as a list, required and supplied optional parameters are set from argv with JimSetProcArg, and unsupplied optional parameters get their default values with Jim_SetVariable; a failure while binding jumps to the cleanup label with that code. If there is no trace callback or the trace callback (JimTraceCallback "proc") returns JIM_OK it evaluates the body with Jim_EvalObj. At the cleanup label (reached after binding, after a failed trace, and after the body) it runs deferred calls with JimInvokeDefer, restores the parent frame and frees the call frame with JimFreeCallFrame (reuse flag); then, if the code is JIM_RETURN, it decrements interp->returnLevel and, when that reaches 0 or below, replaces the code with interp->returnCode and resets returnCode to JIM_OK and returnLevel to 0. It decrements interp->procLevel and returns the code. So the frame and procLevel are only created and decremented on the paths that get past the arity, empty-body and depth checks, and procLevel is incremented before argument binding.
